gloss: go round, surround; strike off, beat down
summary:
A circuit can be a repeated passage round a city or the position of people gathered on every side. In Psalm 17 the people surrounding the speaker threaten his life.

The action removes growth or fruit by a blow. Isaiah’s harvest image directs attention to the few olives still clinging to the branches. The psalm traces the sun across the sky; the other three passages use a turning point to mark elapsed time.

words.gloss: go round, surround; strike or cut off

senses.definition: Isaiah describes the festivals returning as year succeeds year.
Israel’s fighting men make a circuit of Jericho. Worshippers are invited to walk around Zion and count its towers.
David says his enemies surround him. The verb also describes troops taking up positions around a city or a king.
The command about the hair at the sides of the head forbids rounding off its edges.
Isaiah pictures an iron implement cutting down the dense growth of the forest. Job uses the verb of his own skin in a difficult description of its destruction.
Isaiah pairs a rope with the belt it displaces as the women of Zion exchange ornaments for signs of distress.
Both passages compare the few who remain after judgment to the olives left on the tree after the branches have been beaten.
The sun sets out from one end of the heavens and makes its circuit to their other end.
The ingathering festival marks the turn of the year. The word also marks the passage of the days before Hannah bears Samuel and the return of the campaigning season.

evidence.locator: נְקַף II, Afel אַקֵּף, Targum Judges 11:18 on Israel going around Edom
נְקַף I, Targum Onkelos Exodus 34:20 and Eruvin 53b on a ladle striking a jug

note:
The Syriac verb ܢܩܦ means to adhere or follow (SEDRA lexeme 2027; Acts 8:13). Its relationship to making a circuit is uncertain. The Hebrew striking verb has its own entry.

The striking and encircling verbs have identical written forms. The object and the action in each passage guide the choice between them.

Merged from `naqaph`, `naqaph-strike` on 2026-11-20: one root, one entry.

Added 2026-11-21: תְּקוּפָה, from its former one-word entry. Filed under נקף 'go round': scripture uses the verb of the year's circuit (Isa 29:1 חַגִּים יִנְקֹפוּ, 'let the feasts go round'), as תְּקוּפָה is used of the turn of the year (Exo 34:22, 1Sa 1:20) and the sun's circuit (Psa 19:7). The noun's shape, with no doubling, is that of a by-form קוּף.

Its former note: The biblical contexts establish the spatial and temporal senses. They do not by themselves fix a technical astronomical date for the festival.
